questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I always wanted to study in France, since I learned French in my gap year. I had a better chance to be accepted in Sorbonne, since there were more people who could go there from UCPH. I also wanted to challenge myself and speak/live and study in French. Sorbonne University also had a great reputation in France, so looking for a job in France in the future, it would look good on my CV. A lot of my professors have written acknowledged books/papers and writes articles in the French press, which was reassuring, that I made the right choice with the academic standards the history program has to offer.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Some students occupied the university in April, so some weeks were on Zoom. This worked well, just a bit of a shame to not have the 'full' experience there. In total, I had two professors during the semester, who only did Zoom university. I think the experience is what you make it - they had Erasmus-parties, but people who study their bachelor (license) in France are mostly 18-21 years old. They had other activities and trips you could choose as well as an international student (catered to first comers in Paris)

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: The information was there - it just came late and it was hard to find. Search for 'Coordinateurs/ Coordinatrices pédagogiques' and there will be a pdf-file and other documents to read. When choosing courses, you need to have at least 50% of your courses at your UFR (department). So, you can't study philosophy, art, history, literature, etc at the same time. What I would advice you to do is to choose 1 UFR to limit the administrative problems that you WILL fase. I had 6 courses (30 ECTS) in the History department (must have at least 2 different time-periodes).

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I got an email saying where I should go to sign the arrival paper. There was an Erasmus-student welcoming team to greet us and tell us about their activities too. I also got helps from other international students.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: Never expect to get an answer for an email. Always try to find a place where you can meet the actual people. In the first few weeks, there was 1 weekly time slot to have a face to face conversation about your issue. I got the email for where I should go in January. No information before that.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I used an agency. You need a garant. It's expensive but saved me a lot of worrying and it was fairly easy.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: No matter where you live, you can save money by having lunch at the Crous-restaurants (3-4€) around town. It might also be ideal if you don't really have a kitchen. I lived central and could walk to Sorbonne, this is ideal for when there are strikes in the metro/bus line, but this rarely happens long-term. I really enjoyed having my own place, I know most people have a roomie.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: No comments as I wasn't interested.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Many informations came AFTER I did the Online Learning Agreement, so I learned the hard way that 50% of your courses should be at that 1 UFR and it need to be the same courses. I received my Erasmus-scholarship in March because I had to deal with the administration at Sorbonne and Copenhagen. You can always change your OLA, but please be aware of the 'forhåndsgodkendelse' needs to be re-applied for if you change your courses. This is pretty normal, since Sorbonne publish their courses very late. Again - patience is key - but it's a struggle.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You go to the Erasmus-office and get signed 'proof of arrival' or at least just to get your student card. Then you sign a paper within the first week or two of all the courses you have chosen. You chose the courses WHEN you are there mostly. You need to talk to the teacher and often write your name on a list to be sure that you have registered for the class. For some courses, there are too many students, and Erasmus-students can't reserve them online (like the French). When you have chosen them, you need to write them with the course number, ECTS points, name of the teachers and then get a signature from the head of the UFR (again - you can either arrange a meeting or show up on the 1 time a week they are open for students). Then you are set. The most important thing is to get your name on the list of the classes called the TD, which is the 'practical' class.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: There was a pdf file on the site of the UFR.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all the classes that I wanted - but I also knew I could only choose once I was there, so I didn't set my self up for anything specific.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Be patience. You might need to hand in a new OLA and a new 'forhåndgodkendelse' - it will take time, but you will succeed if you are persistent. Please note you will not receive your Erasmus-scholarship before this is settled.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I had some very interesting courses - 6 different ones. Every class had a TD and a CM. One if listening and one is practical - where you hand in 1 assignment, 1 presentation and maybe also one longer group project. It's not really that engaging of an environment - no time for group discussions in all your classes. You typically hear presentations and then the teacher talks the rest of the time. In the CM, it's only the teacher that talks.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I did not find it to be too hard or too easy, yet I found the level of French to be hard in some classes. You will succeed if you take notes and prepare for the classes and mostly just focus on your own presentation or assignment.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: There was no individual research projects, I only had 2 group projects. You work mostly by yourself. You sit and write notes and it's not the same 'relax' atmosphere as at UCPH. You can ask to tape the teacher so that you can listen to it again. Most other students would also happily send you notes, since it's pretty hard to listen (and understand) and write proper notes. There are many deadlines (presentations, assignments, group assignment). At University of Copenhagen you mostly need to do 1-2 deadlines pr. semester, where I had 12 different in the span of 3 months. This can be 20-30 minute PP or 8-10 pages papers. Every course also have a Devoir Sur table (DST) - which is a 2-hour test you must do at the university. Some teachers know your level of French isn't the same, so they won't count it in your final note (Controle Continue). They also check if you are present at the University. You can only be absent 3 times (pr. class) without any reasoning - you need a medical note afterwards.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
1. Histoire des mondes germaniques: L'Allemagne à l'heure des empires 1806-1989
2. Histoire de la construction européenne
3. 1914-1918 et sa mémoire. Approche sociale et culturelle
4. La consommation de masse au XXe siècle 
5. Histoire de l'extrême droite en France
6. Histoire de la démographie et de la famille en France

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Histoire de la démographie et de la famille en France - really interesting perspective on French family construction. The teacher was also very nice and welcoming.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I have no idea how much money I spend on food and personal belongings. This is very much up to the individual. You can find hot student-meals for 3-4€ at Crous, you can cook at home, but you can also expect to use 15-50€ when you go to a restaurant.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
I don't think there is a major difference in the life at Copenhagen and Paris - if you need to find student bars/offers you will, but if you want to go somewhere trendy/hipster then it cost more. It's a personal choice. 
The housing insurance was inexpensive - use the ADH - assurances etudiants . I paid the same amount for 6 months as I do for 1 month in CPH.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I did not research it or use it.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: They did some tours around the city, they had Erasmus-parties and they had some trips you could pay for. There are also other organisations outside of Sorbonne that does this.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: It's great to at least go to the Erasmus-parties once to see if you like the atmosphere. I would recommend the friday bar at Frederikskirken, where they have different activities - often with beers and food. There are many other young Danes that go there to find a network in Paris.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Use your student ID to go for free at the museum. Do picnics in the parks and enjoy the city slow paced. Also try to get the SNCF Carte Avantage Jeune so that you can buy train tickets with a big discount and explore more of France. With the Paris metro card, you can still explore a lot of the smaller villages around Paris for free. Flixbus is also recommended.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was frustrating at first with the administration, but once you have just realized that it's inefficient, you will take it more casual - this goes for housing, university etc. You also need to be very formal with the teachers or strangers you meet.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Again - they are much younger than the students from UCPH, so it's up to you if you feel like it. They are nice and helpful. Many of them are very motivated and you could get a lot of inspiration from their career steps, since French students are very much into internships and being proactive with their career moves even at a young age. Also, go to student events outside of Sorbonne, there you will find international or French students as well.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Administration. The formal tone. The fact that you cannot discuss with your teacher or co-students. There is no individual research in the 'real world', it's very much just sources in books etc.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I really enjoyed that you could talk French, sit at bars, visit museums and enjoy the Parisian life as a local student - much easier to meet people when you feel confident in French. I love the fact that you could explore multiple neighborhoods and actually have time to see more than the Louvre, Eiffel Tower and Montmartre.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Be patience - it will be worth it - but the administration is a nightmare and you just have to do it. 
2. Be prepared for many deadlines - it's going to be intense. 
3. Never expect to get an answer on email, always go directly to meet them.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Talk to other exchange students to find help, you are all in it together. I would also recommend to stay with one UFR.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: It was very rewarding to study at one of the top universities (in humanities) in France and in French. Your French level will improve. I also found it to be such a unique experience to have the possibility to live in Paris 'with a purpose' and can put it on your CV. You will meet many other international students and have so many new memories with your friends in Paris.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The language in some of my courses. It was tough, but you just have to tape it or do some extra research on the topic.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: It's not easy to go on exchange, there is a lot of paperwork, but it has been one of the best parts of my bachelor despite that. Paris is what you make it - go out and make friends in the city, and you will feel a quicker connection to the city. If you have the possibility - save up a lot of money before going - Paris is much more fun, when you can afford to live there.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
